pages.name: The star of windings
pages.text: This picture draws the supply's three windings as a phasor star. Each arrow runs from the star point to a line, L1, L2 or L3. Its length is that winding's voltage, 254 V. The faint triangle joins the line ends. Its sides are the voltages between lines. The loads take their supply across them. Every length in this picture is a voltage.

pages.name: Between two lines
pages.task: Each winding gives 254 V. What does a voltmeter read between two lines, such as L1 and L2?
pages.why: The line voltage is 1.732 times the phase voltage, so 254 × 1.732 = 440 V. That is each side of the triangle.

pages.name: The hull as a dot
pages.text: Now add the hull as a dot. The hull is earth. A voltmeter from each line to the dot reads that line's voltage to earth. With no fault the dot sits at the star point, so each line reads 254 V. No wire ties the hull to the star point. Each line leaks to the hull a little through its cable's capacitance. The three leaks are equal, so they hold the hull at the middle of the star.

pages.name: Before the fault
pages.task: L1 faults solidly to the hull. What will the voltmeters on L2 and L3 read?
pages.why: The fault puts the hull at L1's potential. L2 is still 440 V from L1, so it reads 440 V to earth. So does L3.

pages.task: A solid first fault on L1 draws only a small current. What has it changed that matters?
pages.answer: L2 and L3 now sit at 440 V to earth, so their insulation is stressed harder
pages.why: A tiny current can still move the earth a long way. The hull now sits at L1, so L2 and L3 are 440 V from it. Their insulation holds that until someone clears the fault.

pages.name: A 400 V supply
pages.task: An insulated 400 V supply has 231 V a phase. L3 faults solidly to earth. What do the three lines read to earth?
pages.why: The hull takes L3's potential, so L3 reads 0 V. L1 and L2 are a full line voltage from L3, so each reads 400 V. That is 231 × 1.732, √3 times the phase voltage. The picture stays on its 440 V supply, so its healthy lines read 440 V, not 400 V.

pages.name: The first fault
pages.task: An insulated 440 V board gets its first solid earth fault, on L1. What do you expect?
pages.answer: Nothing trips, the motors run on, and L2 and L3 read 440 V to earth
pages.why: The hull moves to L1, so L1 reads 0 V and the others 440 V. The motors see only the line voltages, which do not change. The fault passes only a small current, so nothing trips. The board runs on. Its insulation takes the extra stress until someone finds the fault.
